The appellants' predecessors also referred to maps consistent with the respondents' map. The plaintiffs alleged encroachment by the defendants, and the Subordinate Judge and High Court found in their favor. The appellants filed an appeal by certificate, indicating they believe the High Court made an error in judgment.

label: allowed
rationale: The Government's justification for reducing the retirement age is questionable, as the Pay Commission's recommendation on age was not binding and the reduction was a policy decision. The Government's actions may be seen as arbitrary and in violation of Articles 14, 16, 21, and 300A of the Constitution. The Ordinance's retrospective deletion of the proviso to Rule 2 of the Fundamental Rules also raises concerns about the validity of the reduction.

label: allowed
rationale: The case facts indicate that the Income Tax Officer initially assessed the amounts received by the heirs as a Hindu Undivided Family for 1950-51 and 1951-52, but the Appellate Tribunal held they were not income of the HUF. Subsequently, the Income Tax Officer initiated proceedings under Section 34 of the Income Tax Act, treating the entity as 'Amarchand N. Shroff by his heirs and legal representatives' (an individual) and assessing the amounts under Section 24B. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that valid notice under Section 34 could only be served for 1950-51, quashing assessments for subsequent years. The Appellate Tribunal upheld the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, holding that Section 24B did not apply to income received after Amarchand's death and that the receipts were capital in nature. The High Court answered the referred question in the negative, holding the sums were not assessable to income tax in the hands of the heirs under Section 24B. The Commissioner of Income Tax appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that Section 24B deemed the amounts received by heirs after death as income of the deceased, liable to tax to the extent of the estate. This suggests that the appeal is likely to be allowed, as the Commissioner is arguing for the application of Section 24B.

label: allowed
rationale: The petitioners are daily-rated carpenters employed by the Corporation, which is a company incorporated under the Companies Act with the primary object of preserving traditional arts and crafts. The Corporation maintains only administrative staff in production centers, employing no permanent craftsmen. The petitioners filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution seeking enforcement of the fundamental right to 'equal pay for equal work' compared to regular carpenters in Government service. The Corporation contends that the petitioners are industrial workmen treated as construction workers, paid minimum wages applicable to the construction industry, and provided with tools and uniforms. However, the Corporation states that there are no regular employees in the petitioners' category within its establishment, so the question of parity with regular employees does not arise internally. The petitioners are covered under the Bonus Act and the Employees' Provident Fund Act. Given the circumstances, it is more likely that the appeal or petition will be allowed, as the petitioners are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to equal pay for equal work.

label: allowed
rationale: The Central Government specified 50 'All India Tourist Vehicle Permits' to be granted by the Karnataka State Transport Authority under Section 63(7) of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The proviso to Section 63(7) was introduced by the Amending Act 47 of 1978, mandating preference for applications from the India Tourism Development Corporation, State Tourism Development Corporations, State Tourist Departments, and operators approved by the Central Government. The Karnataka State Transport Authority granted 11 permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, one to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation, and two to the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation. The Karnataka State Transport Appellate Tribunal set aside the grants to the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and three permits to the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation. The Tribunal granted three permits to private operators and increased the Indian Tourism Development Corporation's permits to three. The Tribunal held that the rule of preference required the exclusion of 'non-preferred' applicants because the number of preferred applicants exceeded the available permits. The High Court of Karnataka rejected writ petitions challenging the Tribunal's order, upholding the view that preference mandated the exclusion of non-preferred classes when sufficient preferred applicants were available. The High Court distinguished the Supreme Court's decision in Sher Singh vs Union of India, arguing that the context of Chapter IV differed from Chapter IV-A of the Act. Appeals were filed by the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation, and private operators, challenging the interpretation of the proviso and the constitutionality of clause (iv) of the proviso.

label: allowed
rationale: The petitioners have successfully challenged the rejection of their applications for registration as Export Houses and for Additional licences under the Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March 1979. The Supreme Court's decision in Union of India vs Rajnikant Brothers has been followed by the Bombay High Court, which ordered the authorities to grant Export House Certificates and Additional licences to the petitioners. The petitioners have also filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of Para 218(10) of the 1988-91 Policy as arbitrary and discriminatory under Article 14. The petitioners have been granted Additional licences dated November 16, 1987, and August 31, 1987, valid for 12 months, based on the 1978-79 Policy. The value of these licences was calculated at one-third of the f.o.b. value of exports made in 1977-78. The petitioners were unable to utilize the licences fully before their expiry on March 31, 1988. The Government issued the revised Import & Export Policy for the period April 1988 to March 1991, which introduced new eligibility criteria based on Net Foreign Exchange (NFE) earnings and granted specific import flexibilities to Export Houses under Para 215. However, Para 218(10) of the 1988-91 Policy provided that Additional licences issued prior to April 1, 1988, or issued on exports from 1986-87 or earlier, would not be eligible for the import flexibilities available under the new Policy. The petitioners have filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the validity of Para 218(10) as arbitrary and discriminatory under Article 14. The Additional licences granted to the petitioners expired during the pendency of the writ petitions.
